title: A 15-line Python check for credit-based AI pricing: plan credits, top-ups and rollover
author: FIRAT
summary: Most AI tools now bill in credits. The pricing page shows a monthly fee, but three other numbers decide what you really pay: the cost of one plan credit, the cost of a top-up credit, and what happens to credits you do not use. Here is a small script that turns a pricing table into those numbers, with one live example. The example AI Flow Chat is a no-code canvas for AI content workflows. Its prices, read on aiflowchat.com on 26 November 2026 (USD, monthly billing): Plan Price Credits Rollover Top-up Basic $29 8,000 none listed $6 per 1,000 Scale $59 18,000 50% $6 per 1,000 Pro $119 40,000 100% $6 per 2,000 The script plans = { "Basic" : dict ( price = 29 , credits = 8_000 , topup_usd = 6 , topup_credits = 1_000 ) , "Scale" : dict ( price = 59 , credits = 18_000 , topup_usd = 6 , topup_credits = 1_000 ) , "Pro" : dict ( price = 119 , credits = 40_000 , topup_usd = 6 , topup_credits = 2_000 ) , } def per_1k ( usd , credits ) : return usd / credits * 1_000 for name , p in plans . items ( ) : plan_rate = per_1k ( p [ "price" ] , p [ "credits" ] ) topup_rate = per_1k ( p [ "topup_usd" ] , p [ "topup_credits" ] ) print ( f "{name:6} plan ${plan_rate:.2f}/1k top-up ${topup_rate:.2f}/1k " f "top-up premium {topup_rate / plan_rate - 1:+.0%}" ) def effective_rate ( price , used ) : """Cost per 1,000 credits you actually used in a month with no rollover.""" return per_1k ( price , used ) print ( f "Basic at half usage: ${effective_rate(29, 4_000):.2f}/1k" ) Output: Basic plan $3.62/1k top-up $6.00/1k top-up premium +66% Scale plan $3.28/1k top-up $6.00/1k top-up premium +83% Pro plan $2.98/1k top-up $3.00/1k top-up premium +1% Basic at half usage: $7.25/1k What the numbers say The plan discount is small. The largest plan is about 18% cheaper per credit than the smallest. On its own that rarely justifies a jump of two tiers. Top-ups are where the price doubles. On the two smaller plans a top-up credit costs 66% to 83% more than a plan credit. Five top-ups on Basic cost $30 for 5,000 credits; moving up one plan costs $30 and adds 10,000. Unused credits are the hidden cost. Use half of a plan with no rollover and your real rate doubles. If your workload comes in bursts, a plan that carries credits over can beat a cheaper plan that resets to zero. Use it on any tool Replace the dictionary with the plans of the tool you are comparing. Then answer three questions before you pay: How many credits does one unit of your real work cost? Measure it in the trial. Do unused credits expire at the end of the month? What is the top-up rate next to the plan rate? We keep dated price readings for a few hundred AI and SaaS tools as an open CSV, if you want more tables to run this on: https://kuponaut.com/ai-tool-pricing-statistics/ Disclosure: Kuponaut is an AI Flow Chat affiliate partner and may earn a commission if you buy through our site. Prices were read on the company's own page on 26 November 2026. This post was drafted with AI assistance and the arithmetic was checked by running the script.

title: Datacenter, IPv6, Residential or Mobile: Which Proxy Do You Actually Need?
author: ProxyZen
summary: If you've ever built a scraper that worked perfectly on your laptop and then died on CAPTCHAs in production, or lost a batch of social accounts the day after creating them, the problem was probably the proxy type, not the code. Here's a practical guide to choosing the right one. The four proxy types Datacenter IPv4. IPs from hosting providers. Fast, stable and cheap. A private (dedicated) IPv4 is used only by you, so nobody else ruins its reputation. Good for social media, ad accounts, SEO tools and most websites. Datacenter IPv6. Same idea, but the IPv6 address space is practically unlimited, so IPs cost cents. The catch: not every site supports IPv6. Google, YouTube, Instagram, Facebook and Telegram do; many smaller sites don't. Test your target before buying a large batch. Residential. IPs of real home internet users. To the target site you look like a regular visitor from a specific country or city. Usually billed per GB. Use them when datacenter IPs get blocked: marketplaces, heavily protected sites, geo-specific ad verification. Mobile (4G/5G). Carrier IPs. Hundreds of real subscribers share one mobile IP through carrier-grade NAT, so platforms almost never ban them outright. The most expensive option, but the most trusted. Quick decision table Use case Proxy type Managing 5–50 social accounts Private IPv4, one IP per account Ad accounts (Meta, Google, TikTok) IPv4 or mobile Bulk account creation Mobile or rotating residential Scraping Google / YouTube at scale IPv6 Scraping Amazon, eBay and other marketplaces Residential Rank tracking by city Residential with city targeting Antidetect browser profiles IPv4 or sticky residential Rotating vs sticky sessions Rotating : a new IP on every request. Ideal for scraping, since blocks never accumulate on a single address. Sticky : the same IP for 1–60 minutes. Required for logged-in sessions, because a login that jumps between countries looks suspicious. Many providers let you switch modes right in the proxy username, for example: user-country-de-city-berlin-session-abc123:password@gate.example.com:8080 Using a proxy in Python import requests proxy = "http://USER:PASS@HOST:PORT" r = requests . get ( "https://api.ipify.org?format=json" , proxies = { "http" : proxy , "https" : proxy } , timeout = 15 , ) print ( r . json ( ) ) # should print the proxy IP, not yours For SOCKS5, install requests[socks] and use socks5h://USER:PASS@HOST:PORT . The h makes DNS resolve through the proxy too, so your real DNS server doesn't leak. Check a proxy before you trust it Does it work, and which IP does it show? Run the snippet above or use any proxy checker. Fraud score and blacklists. If the IP is already flagged, accounts on it won't last long. WebRTC leak. In a browser, WebRTC can expose your real IP even behind a proxy. Timezone and language match. A German IP with a browser set to Asia/Tokyo is a red flag for antifraud systems. You can run all of these for free at proxyzen.net/en/tools/ip-check and proxyzen.net/en/tools/proxy-checker . Provider checklist Dedicated or shared? For accounts, always dedicated. Automatic delivery in seconds, or manual? Can you renew the same IP? Short rental periods for testing (days, not months)? Does residential traffic expire at the end of the month? Replacement or refund policy? A REST API for automation? TL;DR Accounts → private IPv4. Big scraping on Google/YouTube → IPv6. Protected sites and marketplaces → residential. Maximum trust → mobile. Always check fraud score and WebRTC before use. I run ProxyZen , a proxy service, and wrote this after answering the same questions from our customers again and again. If you want to try it, there's a public API with code examples on GitHub . Questions are welcome in the comments.

title: data science certification worth it
author: Ashutosh Upadhyay
summary: Determining whether data science with python certification depends on a candidate's career stage, target role, and willingness to pair formal credentials with verifiable technical work. Across enterprise analytics, financial services, healthcare, cloud operations, and cybersecurity, organizations evaluate data practitioners on problem-solving ability, statistical judgment, and system reliability rather than certificates alone. Because training options range from self-paced introductory courses to proctored cloud and analytics exams, treating every credential as equal creates unrealistic expectations. Examining how hiring teams view credentials, where certificates add practical structure, and when hands-on evidence carries greater weight provides a clear basis for deciding whether a data science certification worth it aligns with individual goals. How Hiring Teams Evaluate Data Science Credentials Recruitment processes in analytics and machine learning typically separate resume screening from technical evaluation. Each stage weights credentials differently depending on the role and organizational maturity. Resume Screening and Role Alignment Automated screening systems and recruiters often look for recognizable tools, foundational coursework, and platform familiarity when filtering high volumes of applications. A recognized credential from an established cloud, data platform, or analytics organization can help signal structured study—especially for applicants transitioning from adjacent functions or early-career roles. Technical Interviews and Practical Proof Technical interviewers and hiring managers focus on how a candidate frames ambiguous questions, handles messy data, validates models, and explains trade-offs. Passing an exam or finishing a course rarely substitutes for demonstrating clean code, thoughtful experiment design, and realistic error analysis during technical discussions. When a Certification Adds Practical Value A credential tends to deliver higher value when it addresses a specific gap in structure, platform familiarity, or role transition rather than serving as a shortcut around practical execution. Structured Learning for Career Switchers and Beginners Professionals moving from spreadsheets, operations, software engineering, or project management often benefit from a sequenced syllabus covering programming, data manipulation, statistics, and modeling. A structured program provides milestones and guided exercises that reduce blind spots for learners starting from scratch. Cloud and Enterprise Platform Validation For practitioners working on cloud infrastructure or enterprise data platforms, vendor or platform credentials can verify familiarity with managed pipelines, model training workflows, and deployment tooling. In organizations standardized on specific cloud or lakehouse ecosystems, platform knowledge often aligns closely with day-to-day engineering requirements. A simple diagram here can illustrate how a candidate's baseline experience, target role requirements, and portfolio projects interact with certification value across career stages. When Credentials Offer Limited Return Even well-designed courses and exams have clear boundaries in how much career leverage they provide on their own. Passive Course Completion Without Applied Work Certificates earned purely through video viewing or basic multiple-choice quizzes rarely demonstrate readiness for real datasets with missing values, class imbalance, or shifting distributions. Hiring panels generally place greater weight on reproducible projects that show how a candidate solved end-to-end problems. Over-Indexing on Volume Over Relevance Collecting numerous overlapping certificates across similar introductory topics rarely improves hiring outcomes. Depth in core analytical workflows, clear communication of findings, and alignment with target job descriptions typically carry more weight than a long list of credentials. This comparison is best represented using table contrasting scenarios where a certification provides strong supporting value against scenarios where alternative investments yield higher return. Career Scenario Role of Certification Higher-Priority Complement or Alternative Early-Career or Career Switcher Provides structured curriculum and basic credibility End-to-end portfolio projects showing data cleaning, modeling, and evaluation Cloud or MLOps-Oriented Role Validates familiarity with cloud ML or data workflows Hands-on pipeline building, testing, and deployment experience Experienced Practitioner (3+ Years) Optional validation for unfamiliar cloud or governance frameworks Proven business impact, cross-functional leadership, and production track record Budget- or Time-Constrained Learner Selective focus on high-alignment exams or low-cost tracks Targeted practice on SQL, statistics, Python workflows, and case studies Comparing Credential Formats and Costs Credentials in the analytics and machine learning space generally fall into distinct categories, each with different time commitments, exam formats, and verification standards. Guided Course and Specialization Certificates Online courses and multi-course specializations typically emphasize foundational instruction, coding labs, and graded assignments. They are widely accessible in terms of cost and pacing, making them practical for building core vocabulary and introductory workflows. Proctored Technical and Analytics Exams Proctored exams administered by cloud providers, software vendors, or professional bodies test applied knowledge under time and supervision constraints. Because these assessments often require preparation across architecture, evaluation, or domain standards, they are typically suited to learners who already possess baseline technical familiarity. A chart here can illustrate how typical preparation time, cost ranges, and technical prerequisites differ across foundational coursework, intermediate platform exams, and advanced or specialized credentials. Practical Criteria for Making the Decision Evaluating whether a data science certification worth it becomes more straightforward when anchored to concrete career criteria rather than general market trends. Questions to Weigh Before Enrolling Target Job Alignment: Do target job descriptions for desired roles regularly reference specific cloud, analytics, or governance competencies covered by the credential? Skill Gap Closure: Does the program teach skills not yet practiced in current coursework or workplace responsibilities? Practical Assessment: Does the path require building models, writing queries, or analyzing realistic scenarios rather than relying solely on recall? Time and Cost Trade-Off: Can the required study hours and exam fees be justified alongside time spent building projects and preparing for interviews? Conclusion Deciding whether a 8 best data science certification to boost your career comes down to viewing credentials as a supporting signal rather than a standalone qualification. When paired with hands-on projects, sound statistical reasoning, and clear communication of business trade-offs, a relevant certification can provide structure, validate platform skills, and support career transitions. When pursued in isolation from real problem solving, however, its practical impact remains limited.

title: Comparing Leading AI Frameworks for Enterprise Performance
author: Sam Amderson
summary: An enterprise AI frameworks comparison usually ranks tools by features or raw speed, and that is why the results mislead. Speed barely separates the leading options, because the model call dominates each run. In one recent benchmark, six mainstream frameworks averaged between 6.79 and 8.39 seconds per run. What separates them is behavior under failure: repeated steps, wasted tokens and lost state. This guide defines four measures that expose those gaps, checks five frameworks against them, and ends with a complete Python scorecard that you can run on your own workload data. What Should an Enterprise AI Frameworks Comparison Actually Measure? A fair enterprise AI frameworks comparison starts with the unit of work, not the token. Enterprises pay for finished tasks. A run that loops, fails or loses state still spends money and delivers nothing. So the sheet needs measures tied to completed outcomes, collected over many runs on the same model and the same tasks. Use four measures, and treat them as a framework selection scorecard: Cost per successful task: total spend divided by successful runs. Failed and repeated runs raise it. Repeat-step rate: the share of runs where the agent repeated a step or a tool call. Crash recovery rate: the share of injected crashes where the run resumed from saved state instead of restarting. Governance overhead: the extra seconds per run once tracing, approvals and audit logging are switched on. The last measure matters more than teams expect. Oversight should scale with autonomy. A read-only agent needs light review, while an agent with production write access needs audit trails, approval gates and rollback controls. Each control, from observability tracing to human-in-the-loop approval, adds latency and code. Measure that cost per framework, along with token overhead from extra prompts and traces, so the cheapest option on paper does not become the most expensive after your security team signs off. Quick check: Is cost per token the same as cost per successful task? No. Token cost counts every run, including the ones that fail or loop. Cost per successful task divides total spend by finished runs, so wasted attempts show up in the number. How Do LangGraph, CrewAI, Microsoft Agent Framework, OpenAI Agents SDK and Google ADK Compare? The table summarizes what each project's official documentation says about orchestration, state and built-in controls. It does not rank them, because the right ranking depends on your measures and your weights. Framework Orchestration model State and recovery Built-in controls LangGraph Stateful graphs Checkpointer plus thread ID; persistent store needed in production Human-in-the-loop through checkpoints CrewAI Flows control the app; Crews run role-based agents State management inside Flows Enterprise security features listed Microsoft Agent Framework Graph workflows: sequential, concurrent, branching Workflow checkpointing; sessions for agents Human-in-the-loop, telemetry; docs describe a public preview OpenAI Agents SDK Agents with handoffs Sessions for working memory; durable runs need an external engine Guardrails, tracing, human-in-the-loop, MCP Google ADK Sequential, loop, parallel and graph workflows Sessions with rewind and migration Evaluation tooling, MCP support, A2A Public numbers add context. Any AI agent framework benchmark has limits, and AIMultiple ran 6,500 runs across 13 frameworks on one model in October 2026. Among four of the five frameworks above, average cost per 1,000 runs ranged from $1.48 for Google ADK to $1.88 for Microsoft Agent Framework. Failure behavior varied far more than cost. In that benchmark, 64% of Microsoft Agent Framework runs hit an error and repeated steps, while Google ADK never repeated a step on one task. Those results come from one model and five tasks. Treat them as a prompt to test, not a verdict. Quick check: Should one public benchmark decide the choice? No. A single benchmark fixes one model, one dataset and one set of tasks. Your tools and failure modes differ, so use it to shortlist candidates and then score your own runs. How Do You Score Frameworks Against Your Own Workload? Public benchmarks cannot know your tools, your data or your failure modes, and enterprise AI framework performance depends on all three. Run the same workflow through each candidate, log every run and score the logs. The script below turns run records into the four measures, scales each one from 0 to 1, applies weights and ranks the frameworks. Change the weights to match your risk. A regulated team might weight recovery and governance above cost. """Weighted scorecard for comparing AI agent frameworks on your own workload. Input: one record per run, per framework. Replace make_sample_runs with your own logs. Metrics (all computed per framework): cost_per_success total spend divided by successful runs (lower is better) repeat_rate share of runs that repeated a step (lower is better) recovery_rate share of injected crashes the run resumed from (higher is better) governance_cost extra seconds per run with tracing and approvals on (lower is better) """ import random from dataclasses import dataclass WEIGHTS = { "cost_per_success" : 0.35 , "repeat_rate" : 0.25 , "recovery_rate" : 0.25 , "governance_cost" : 0.15 , } LOWER_IS_BETTER = { "cost_per_success" , "repeat_rate" , "governance_cost" } @dataclass class Run : framework : str success : bool cost_usd : float repeated_step : bool crash_injected : bool resumed_after_crash : bool seconds_plain : float seconds_governed : float def make_sample_runs ( seed : int = 7 , n : int = 100 ) -> list [ Run ] : """Illustrative placeholder data. It is not a benchmark of any real framework.""" rng = random . Running it prints one summary line per framework, then the ranking: framework_a: cost/success=$0.0017 repeat=8% recovery=97% governance=+0.58s framework_b: cost/success=$0.0017 repeat=38% recovery=50% governance=+1.39s framework_c: cost/success=$0.0021 repeat=22% recovery=79% governance=+0.92s 1. framework_a score=1.00 2. framework_c score=0.38 3. framework_b score=0.34 The same four measures work when you weigh a framework build against a platform-led option, as in the debate over AI-native engineering vs traditional development . Score both on one sheet, with the same weights, so the result stays honest. Quick check: How many runs per framework are enough? AIMultiple used 100 runs per task per framework. Use that as a floor for stable rates, and rerun after every version bump, because behavior changes between releases. Which Failure Modes Only Appear in Production? Production AI agent frameworks face failure modes that demos hide, and three of them matter most. Each one raises cost per successful task while leaving the average latency chart unchanged. First, repeated steps. In the AIMultiple data, CrewAI repeated steps in 85% of Task 5 runs, and the longest LangGraph Task 3 run made 25 tool calls, 16 of them repeats. Second, retry loops that multiply cost. An academic benchmark for AI-native systems found that self-healing mechanisms can act as cost multipliers on unviable workflows. Cap retries per task and alert on token spend per run. Third, lost state and weak tool-call reliability. LangGraph needs a checkpointer and a thread ID to save state. Production use calls for a persistent store such as PostgresSaver or SqliteSaver, because InMemorySaver loses checkpoints on restart. State checkpointing is the base of durable execution; the OpenAI Agents SDK leaves durable execution to an external engine such as Temporal. Distributed designs add a fourth cost. The same study found that agent-to-agent architectures mask latency but pay a reliability tax. Test for all of these on purpose. Kill a worker mid-run, return a tool error and delay a response, then watch what each framework does. Any serious enterprise AI frameworks comparison includes these fault tests, because they show what the average never will. Quick check: Does a durable checkpointer fix repeated steps? No. A checkpointer restores state after a crash or an approval pause. Repeated steps come from planning and tool use, so only repeat-step rate measured over many runs will catch them. Run Three Fault Tests Before You Commit to a Framework Pick one real workflow and run it through two or three candidates with the same model and the same tools. Log every run. Inject three faults on purpose: a worker crash mid-run, a failing tool and a slow response. Record cost per successful task, repeat-step rate, recovery rate and governance overhead. Set your weights before you look at the totals, so the result reflects your risk and not your hopes. Rerun the test after every major version change, because framework behavior shifts between releases. Weigh vendor lock-in too: open protocols such as MCP lower the cost of leaving. Keep the logs, since an auditor or a CTO will ask how you chose. If a plain function can do the job, skip the framework entirely, as Microsoft's own documentation advises. Then write down the result in one page: the weights, the four measures per framework, and the faults you injected. That page becomes your selection record, and the next team can rerun it instead of starting from opinions.

title: Week 1 of 2027 Starts on January 4: ISO Week Numbers for Business-Day Planning
author: Nomad Wozo
summary: I used to treat week numbers as a solved problem. Store a year and a week, render a planner, ship. Then a deadline labeled "week 1 of 2027" and a deadline labeled "the first week of January" landed on two ranges with no days in common. The gap is ISO week numbering. It's the system Python's date.isocalendar() implements, the one Excel documents as System 2 / ISOWEEKNUM , and it does not follow the calendar year the way a lot of US-style WEEKNUM defaults do. If you plan work in week buckets, that difference shows up right at the year boundary. What an ISO week actually is The current standard is ISO 8601-1:2019 (confirmed in 2024; the full text is paywalled). I am relying here on two public restatements I opened today, which agree with each other: Microsoft's WEEKNUM help calls this System 2: "The week containing the first Thursday of the year is the first week of the year, and is numbered as week 1. This system is the methodology specified in ISO 8601." return_type 21 selects it. ISOWEEKNUM is the dedicated function for the same week number. Python's date.isocalendar() docs say an ISO year "consists of 52 or 53 full weeks," a week "starts on a Monday and ends on a Sunday," and "the first week of an ISO year is the first (Gregorian) calendar week of a year containing a Thursday." Those two rules are equivalent, because an ISO week is always Mondayâ€“Sunday: the week that contains the first Thursday also contains January 4. ISO weekday numbers run Monday = 1 through Sunday = 7, which is not JavaScript's getDay() (Sunday = 0). The 2026â€“2027 boundary, day by day I checked the crossing with Python 3.13. The interesting dates are not January 1 alone: from datetime import date for d in ( date ( 2025 , 12 , 28 ) , date ( 2025 , 12 , 29 ) , date ( 2026 , 1 , 1 ) , date ( 2026 , 1 , 4 ) , date ( 2026 , 12 , 28 ) , date ( 2026 , 12 , 31 ) , date ( 2027 , 1 , 1 ) , date ( 2027 , 1 , 3 ) , date ( 2027 , 1 , 4 ) , date ( 2027 , 1 , 10 ) , ) : y , w , wd = d . isocalendar ( ) print ( d . isoformat ( ) , d . strftime ( "%A" ) , f "{y}-W{w:02d}-{wd}" ) print ( "2026-W53-1" , date . fromisocalendar ( 2026 , 53 , 1 ) ) print ( "2026-W53-7" , date . fromisocalendar ( 2026 , 53 , 7 ) ) print ( "2027-W01-1" , date . fromisocalendar ( 2027 , 1 , 1 ) ) date . fromisocalendar ( 2027 , 53 , 1 ) # ValueError: Invalid week: 53 The output: 2025-12-28 Sunday 2025-W52-7 2025-12-29 Monday 2026-W01-1 2026-01-01 Thursday 2026-W01-4 2026-01-04 Sunday 2026-W01-7 2026-12-28 Monday 2026-W53-1 2026-12-31 Thursday 2026-W53-4 2027-01-01 Friday 2026-W53-5 2027-01-03 Sunday 2026-W53-7 2027-01-04 Monday 2027-W01-1 2027-01-10 Sunday 2027-W01-7 2026-W53-1 2026-12-28 2026-W53-7 2027-01-03 2027-W01-1 2027-01-04 Three things in that list surprise people: Monday, December 29, 2025 is already ISO week 1 of 2026 . The ISO year started before New Year's Day. 2026 has a week 53. It runs Monday, December 28, 2026 through Sunday, January 3, 2027. Friday, January 1, 2027 is 2026-W53-5 , not week 1 of 2027. ISO week 1 of 2027 starts on Monday, January 4 . And 2027 has no week 53: date.fromisocalendar(2027, 53, 1) raises ValueError . Nearby years that do have an ISO week 53 are 2015, 2020, 2026, and 2032. Week 53 is not a data-entry bug. Some years just have 53 ISO weeks. The same function also matches examples published on the docs I used: Python's own 2004 walkthrough ( 2003-12-29 is 2004-W01-1 , 2004-01-04 is 2004-W01-7 ), and Microsoft's ISOWEEKNUM example ( 2012-03-09 is ISO week 10, a Friday). Two meanings of "week 1 of 2027" Excel's default WEEKNUM is System 1: "The week containing January 1 is the first week of the year," and the default week begins on Sunday. I did not run Excel. Applying that documented rule to the calendar gives: System 1, week 1 of 2027: Sunday, December 27, 2026 through Saturday, January 2, 2027. ISO week 1 of 2027: Monday, January 4 through Sunday, January 10, 2027. Those ranges do not overlap. January 3, 2027 is in System 1 week 2, and it is still ISO week 53 of 2026. If one team uses Python, ISO-8601 APIs, or ISOWEEKNUM / WEEKNUM(..., 21) , and another uses default WEEKNUM , "ship in week 1" is two different weeks. Even in 2026, where the ranges almost line up, they are not the same. System 1 week 1 of 2026 is December 28, 2025 through January 3, 2026. ISO week 1 of 2026 is December 29, 2025 through January 4, 2026. Each side has one day the other does not. The YEAR() + ISOWEEKNUM() bug A second trap is combining a calendar year with an ISO week number. For January 1, 2027, ISOWEEKNUM should return 53 (same week number as isocalendar() ), and YEAR returns 2027. Stored together, that becomes the key (2027, 53) . That key is invalid: 2027 has only 52 ISO weeks. The ISO year for that Friday is 2026. The safer options I use: Store the ISO year and the ISO week together, not calendar_year + iso_week . Or skip week numbers as a primary key and store the Monday of the week as a date. You can always derive the week label for display. def monday_of_iso_week ( iso_year , week ) : return date . fromisocalendar ( iso_year , week , 1 ) # "Week 53 of 2026" as a concrete range: start = monday_of_iso_week ( 2026 , 53 ) # 2026-12-28 end = date . fromisocalendar ( 2026 , 53 , 7 ) # 2027-01-03 If a ticket says "done in week 53," resolve it to those dates before you count business days inside the week. Counting "five business days in week 1 of 2027" only makes sense after you have agreed which Monday you mean. A JavaScript version that stays in agreement with Python Date still has no built-in ISO week number. This is the function I used. It treats the input as a date-only YYYY-MM-DD in UTC, so a local time zone cannot slide the calendar day. The ISO year is the year of that week's Thursday. Week 1 is the week that contains January 4 of that ISO year. function isoWeek ( isoDate ) { const [ Y , M , D ] = isoDate . split ( "-" ) . map ( Number ) ; const utc = new Date ( Date . UTC ( Y , M - 1 , D ) ) ; const weekday = utc . getUTCDay ( ) === 0 ? 7 : utc . getUTCDay ( ) ; // Mon=1...Sun=7 const thursday = new Date ( utc ) ; thursday . setUTCDate ( utc . getUTCDate ( ) + ( 4 - weekday ) ) ; const isoYear = thursday . getUTCFullYear ( ) ; const jan4 = new Date ( Date . UTC ( isoYear , 0 , 4 ) ) ; const jan4Weekday = jan4 . getUTCDay ( ) === 0 ? 7 : jan4 . getUTCDay ( ) ; const week1Monday = new Date ( jan4 ) ; week1Monday . setUTCDate ( jan4 . getUTCDate ( ) - ( jan4Weekday - 1 ) ) ; const week = Math . round ( ( thursday - week1Monday ) / 86400000 / 7 ) + 1 ; return { isoYear , week , weekday } ; } I compared it with Python's date.isocalendar() on 4,762 consecutive dates, from 2019-12-29 through 2033-01-10, in Node v24.22.1. Zero mismatches, including the 2004 and 2012 documentation examples and the 2020 / 2026 / 2032 week-53 boundaries. What I now do with this If a plan is week-based, I write down the numbering system in the same place as the week number. "ISO 2027-W01" and "the calendar week that contains 2027-01-01" are different instructions. I never store year=2027, week=53 from a calendar date in January. I store the ISO year, or I store a Monday. I don't special-case week 53 away. In 2026 it is a real, seven-day week that happens to straddle New Year's Day. When I need to count business days inside that week, I start from the Monday and Sunday I already resolved, then apply the weekend and holiday rules for that workplace. The week number itself does not know those rules. If you want to see the actual calendar days in a span, I keep a small calculator at WorkdayMap that walks the dates and shows which ones were counted. Sources Fetched 2026-11-25 (Asia/Seoul): ISO 8601-1:2019 catalog page â€” current part of the standard (published 2019, confirmed 2024). Abstract only; full text not retrieved. ISO 8601 overview â€” general date-and-time format page; it does not itself define week 1. Python 3 datetime.date.isocalendar() â€” ISO year / week / weekday rule and the 2004 example. Excel WEEKNUM â€” System 1 vs System 2 (ISO 8601), return_type 21. Excel ISOWEEKNUM â€” ISOWEEKNUM("2012-03-09") documented as 10. Date arithmetic in this post was run on 2026-11-25 (Asia/Seoul) with Python 3.13.5 and Node v24.22.1. I did not execute Excel; the System 1 ranges above follow Microsoft's documented rule applied to those calendar dates.

title: Instant product pages with the Speculation Rules API: an e-commerce playbook
author: not the same
summary: On a store, most navigations are predictable: catalog → product, product → another product, product → back to the catalog. Every one of those clicks normally waits for the network, the server and the render. The Speculation Rules API lets the browser start that work before the click, so the next page appears almost instantly. It's a few lines of JSON, but on a store it needs care. Prerender the wrong URL and you add items to carts, inflate analytics or hammer your server. Here's how we set it up for online stores. 1. Prefetch vs prerender Prefetch downloads the HTML of the next page. Navigation skips the network wait, but the page still renders after the click. Prerender loads and renders the whole page in a hidden tab, scripts included. Navigation is close to instant, but it costs more: CPU, memory, and every request the page makes. For a catalog, prerender on hover is the sweet spot. Prefetch is the safe default everywhere else. 2. Start with document rules and moderate eagerness Instead of listing URLs, let the browser pick links on the page that match a pattern: <script type = "speculationrules" > { "prerender" : [ { "where" : { "and" : [ { "href_matches" : "/product/*" } , { "not" : { "selector_matches" : "[rel~=nofollow]" } } ] } , "eagerness" : "moderate" } ] , "prefetch" : [ { "where" : { "href_matches" : "/category/*" } , "eagerness" : "conservative" } ] } </script> eagerness decides when speculation starts: conservative – on pointer down / touch start; moderate – on hover (desktop) and on pointer down; eager and immediate – as soon as the rule matches. moderate for product links gives a head start of a few hundred milliseconds on desktop without prerendering half the catalog. Chrome also caps how many moderate/conservative prerenders it keeps at once and drops the oldest, so a shopper sweeping the mouse over a grid doesn't load fifty pages. 3. Exclude everything with side effects A prerendered page runs like a real visit. Never speculate on URLs that change state: { "where" : { "and" : [ { "href_matches" : "/*" } , { "not" : { "href_matches" : "/cart*" } } , { "not" : { "href_matches" : "/checkout*" } } , { "not" : { "href_matches" : "/my-account*" } } , { "not" : { "href_matches" : "/*\\?*add-to-cart=*" } } , { "not" : { "href_matches" : "/*logout*" } } ] } , "eagerness" : "conservative" } The classic trap in WooCommerce-style themes is an "Add to cart" link that is a plain <a href="?add-to-cart=123"> . A broad prerender rule turns hovering into adding. Exclude these URLs, or better, make add-to-cart a POST button. 4. Make your own scripts prerender-aware Third-party analytics tags from the big vendors generally wait for activation, but your own code may not. Anything that should only run when a person actually sees the page – view counters, "recently viewed" writes, chat greetings, A/B exposure events – should wait: function whenActivated ( callback ) { if ( document . prerendering ) { document . addEventListener ( 'prerenderingchange' , callback , { once : true } ) ; } else { callback ( ) ; } } whenActivated ( ( ) => { trackProductView ( productId ) ; saveRecentlyViewed ( productId ) ; } ) ; 5. Measure that it works On the destination page you can tell a prerendered navigation by activationStart : const [ nav ] = performance . getEntriesByType ( 'navigation' ) ; const wasPrerendered = nav . activationStart > 0 ; const wasPrefetched = nav . deliveryType === 'navigational-prefetch' ; Send these as a dimension with your page view or LCP data and compare product pages with and without speculation. In Chrome DevTools, Application → Background services → Speculative loads shows which rules matched, what was prerendered and why a speculation failed. 6. If you are on WordPress Since WordPress 6.8, core outputs speculation rules by default: prefetch with conservative eagerness, with cart-like and admin URLs excluded for common setups. That's a good baseline. To move to prerender on hover for products, use the Speculative Loading plugin settings or filter the rules, and keep the exclusions from step 3 for your store's own URLs. Checklist Prerender product links on hover ( moderate ), prefetch the rest on pointer down. Exclude cart, checkout, account, logout and any add-to-cart GET links. Wrap view-tracking and other side effects in a prerenderingchange check. Log activationStart and deliveryType to see the real effect. Check DevTools → Speculative loads after every theme or plugin update. Speculation doesn't fix a slow server or a heavy page, but on a store with a decent baseline it removes most of the wait between "I like this" and "I see it". For the rest of the speed picture, see our PageSpeed optimization guide and website speed and sales . We're not the same , a web development studio from Ukraine working on e-commerce and B2B projects.

title: Why MongoDB Gets Rejected in FYP Proposals (And a Clean 3NF MySQL Schema Instead)
author: Fyp Services
summary: If your FYP proposal says "we will use MongoDB because it is modern and flexible", expect the panel to push back. In Pakistani universities, supervisors and external examiners check your database design against one thing first: normalisation. A document store makes that check almost impossible to pass, because there is no fixed schema to normalise. This is not about MongoDB being bad. It is about what an FYP viva can grade. Why panels reject the MongoDB pitch No schema to examine. The examiner cannot verify 1NF, 2NF and 3NF if every document can have different fields. Duplication by design. Embedding copies of the same student, course or product data in many documents is exactly the redundancy normalisation exists to remove — and viva questions target it. "Flexibility" reads as "we have not designed it yet." Panels hear that sentence from every group, every semester. Unless your project is genuinely document-shaped (logs, sensor data, chat messages at scale) and you can defend that, a relational database is the safer proposal for an FYP. The same system, as a clean 3NF MySQL schema Take a simple FYP example: students submit project proposals, supervisors review them. CREATE TABLE students ( student_id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT , reg_no VARCHAR ( 20 ) UNIQUE NOT NULL , full_name VARCHAR ( 100 ) NOT NULL , email VARCHAR ( 120 ) UNIQUE NOT NULL ) ; CREATE TABLE supervisors ( supervisor_id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT , full_name VARCHAR ( 100 ) NOT NULL , email VARCHAR ( 120 ) UNIQUE NOT NULL , department VARCHAR ( 80 ) NOT NULL ) ; CREATE TABLE proposals ( proposal_id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT , student_id INT NOT NULL , supervisor_id INT NULL , title VARCHAR ( 200 ) NOT NULL , status ENUM ( 'pending' , 'approved' , 'rejected' ) DEFAULT 'pending' , submitted_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP , FOREIGN KEY ( student_id ) REFERENCES students ( student_id ) , FOREIGN KEY ( supervisor_id ) REFERENCES supervisors ( supervisor_id ) ) ; Why this passes the 3NF questions: 1NF: every column holds one value. No comma-separated lists of group members or technologies — those go in their own tables with foreign keys. 2NF: no column depends on only part of a key. Student name lives only in students, never repeated in proposals. 3NF: no column depends on another non-key column. Department belongs to the supervisor record, not copied into every proposal row. The viva questions this prepares you for "Where is your data duplicated?" Nowhere — each fact is stored once, everything else is a foreign key. "What happens if a supervisor changes department?" One row updates, not hundreds. "Show me your ERD." This schema draws directly into an ERD with two clean relationships, which is exactly what Chapter 3 of the report needs. When MongoDB is actually defensible If your core data is unstructured — IoT sensor readings, scraped listings, chat logs — say that, show the document shape, and explain why joins and normalisation do not apply. That answer passes. "It is modern and flexible" does not. For a standard management-system, portal or e-commerce FYP, go relational, normalise to 3NF, and let the examiner's checklist work in your favour.

title: How to Convert a Website Into an App: 5 Real Ways and the Best One
author: Kausar Raza
summary: "Can you turn my website into an app?" is one of the questions I get most from clients. The honest answer is yes, almost always, but "app" can mean five very different things. One costs nothing and takes ten minutes. Another means rebuilding the front end from scratch. Most of the bad advice online comes from mixing them up, or from "free website to app converter" pages that sell you the most expensive one dressed up as the cheapest. Below are the five genuine ways to do it, what each one actually gives you, what the App Store and Google Play will and won't accept, and which one I'd pick for a normal business website. The five ways, side by side Method Where it lives Work involved Best for 1. Installable web app (PWA) Home screen, desktop. No store. A manifest file and icons. Hours. Almost every website, as the first step 2. Trusted Web Activity (TWA) Google Play (Android only) A PWA plus a generated Android package. A day or two. Being findable in Google Play 3. WebView wrapper (Capacitor and similar) Google Play and the App Store A native shell, plus real native features to pass review. Days to weeks. Needing the App Store 4. No-code converter service Both stores A form and a subscription. Days. Content sites with no developer 5. Native or cross-platform rebuild Both stores A new app on your site's API. Weeks to months. Apps people use daily, heavy device features Every option except the last one reuses your existing website. That matters: one codebase means one place to fix a bug, one design to update, and content that changes in the app the moment it changes on the site. Can you turn any website into an app? Technically, yes. Any site that works in a mobile browser can be shown inside an app. Whether it's accepted anywhere is a different question, and the answer depends on the method: Home screen install (PWA): no one approves it. If the site meets the browser's checks, it installs. Google Play: its spam policy rejects apps that are just a website in a WebView, and apps that wrap a website you don't own without the owner's permission. A TWA is Google's own supported route for your own site. Apple App Store: guideline 4.2 (Minimum Functionality) is the one that bites. Apple wants an app to be more than "a repackaged website". A plain wrapper is the classic 4.2 rejection. So "is it possible" is easy. "Is it easy" depends on which store you need, which is the real decision. 1. Make the website installable (a PWA) A progressive web app is just your website with a few extra files that let the browser install it like an app: its own icon on the home screen, its own window with no address bar, its own entry in the app switcher. On a laptop, Chrome and Edge install it as a desktop app too. The minimum is a web app manifest , a small JSON file linked from every page: { "name" : "Your Business Name" , "short_name" : "YourBiz" , "start_url" : "/" , "display" : "standalone" , "background_color" : "#ffffff" , "theme_color" : "#4f46e5" , "icons" : [ { "src" : "/android-chrome-192x192.png" , "sizes" : "192x192" , "type" : "image/png" } , { "src" : "/android-chrome-512x512.png" , "sizes" : "512x512" , "type" : "image/png" } ] } <link rel = "manifest" href = "/site.webmanifest" > <link rel = "apple-touch-icon" href = "/apple-touch-icon.png" > The icons are the fiddly part. Our free favicon generator makes the 192 and 512 px icons, the Apple touch icon and a ready site.webmanifest from one logo, in your browser. What I found when I tested it Older guides say a PWA also needs a service worker before the browser will offer to install it. I checked that on this site. I opened knowledgemarkg.com in Chrome 157 and asked Chrome directly for its installability errors (the same check its install button uses): knowledgemarkg.com: no errors, so it can be installed. It has a manifest like the one above and no service worker at all . example.com , for comparison: no-manifest . No manifest, no install. So for the install prompt in current Chrome, the manifest and icons are what count. A service worker is still worth adding for what it does: it's what lets the app open without a connection, and it's required for push notifications. Without one, an installed app is still online-only. How people install it Android (Chrome): menu → Install app (or Add to Home screen ). iPhone and iPad (Safari): Share → Add to Home Screen . There's no automatic prompt on iOS, so tell people where the button is. Windows and Mac (Chrome or Edge): the install icon at the right of the address bar. Limits worth knowing No store listing. People can't find it by searching Google Play or the App Store. Push on iPhone needs the app installed. Since iOS 16.4, web push works for web apps added to the Home Screen, not for the site in a normal Safari tab, and only after the user taps something like a "Turn on notifications" button. Device access is narrower than a native app (no access to contacts, limited background work, especially on iOS). For a business site, a blog, a booking site or a shop, none of those are usually deal-breakers. That's why this is where I start every time. 2. Put the PWA in Google Play with a Trusted Web Activity A Trusted Web Activity is an Android app whose whole screen is your website, rendered by the user's Chrome (or another supporting browser) instead of a WebView. It's Google's supported way to list your own PWA in Google Play. Because it uses the real browser, logins, cookies and payments behave exactly like the website. The usual route: Get the PWA from step 1 working first. Chrome's TWA guide requires the site to meet the PWA install criteria. Generate the Android package with PWABuilder (a website: paste your URL, download the package) or Bubblewrap (Google's command-line tool, npx @bubblewrap/cli init --manifest=https://yoursite.com/site.webmanifest ). Prove you own the site. The app is matched to the site with Digital Asset Links : a file at /.well-known/assetlinks.json on your domain containing your app's package name and the SHA-256 fingerprint of its signing key. Upload to a Google Play developer account (a one-time $25 registration fee charged by Google). [ { "relation" : [ "delegate_permission/common.handle_all_urls" ] , "target" : { "namespace" : "android_app" , "package_name" : "com.yourbusiness.app" , "sha256_cert_fingerprints" : [ "AB:CD:EF:...:12" ] } } ] Two traps catch nearly everyone: The address bar shows up in the app. That means the asset links check failed, and Chrome falls back to showing your site in a Custom Tab with browser UI. The usual cause is the fingerprint: if Google Play signs the app (Play App Signing), the fingerprint to use is the one from Play Console, not the key on your laptop. The testing rule for new accounts. A personal developer account created after 13 November 2023 has to run a closed test with at least 12 testers, opted in for 14 days in a row, before it can publish to everyone. Plan two weeks for that. There is no TWA for iPhone. Apple has no equivalent, which is why the App Store needs method 3, 4 or 5. 3. Wrap the site in a native shell (Capacitor) A WebView app is a real native app, built in Android Studio and Xcode, whose screen is a web view showing your site or your site's built files. Capacitor (from the Ionic team) is the most common way to do it today. Cordova is the older option, and React Native or Flutter can host a WebView too. Capacitor works two ways: Bundle the front end inside the app. Your built HTML, CSS and JavaScript ship in the app and talk to your server's API. It opens instantly and partly works offline, but every front-end change means a new app release. This suits sites built with React, Vue or a static export of Next.js. Point the app at your live URL (Capacitor's server.url setting). Changes on the site appear in the app at once. Capacitor's own docs describe this setting as meant for live reload during development, not for production, and an app that is only your URL is exactly what Apple's 4.2 review looks for. The point of Capacitor is its plugins: native push notifications, camera, file access, biometrics, share sheet, haptics. Those are also what gets a wrapped website through App Store review. Getting a wrapped site past Apple's 4.2 review Reading the rejection threads on Apple's developer forums, the reasons repeat: the app shows the website's own header and menu, a "download our app" banner, browser-style dead ends and error pages, and nothing a user couldn't get in Safari. What tends to get through is an app that does at least a few things the site can't: Native navigation (a bottom tab bar) instead of the site's hamburger menu, with the site's header and footer hidden inside the app. Native push notifications for something that matters to the user: an order shipped, a booking confirmed. Something that uses the device: scanning, camera upload, Face ID login, offline saved items. A proper offline screen instead of a blank page or a browser error. Apple's developer programme costs $99 a year, and you need a Mac (or a cloud Mac) to build and submit. 4. No-code website-to-app converters Search "website to app converter" and you'll get two very different things: Paid services that build and publish a WebView or native-shell app for you, with push notifications and a native menu, often with a WordPress or Shopify plugin. They're a reasonable choice for a content site with no developer, and the good ones handle the store submissions too. Check three things before paying: who owns the developer accounts (it should be you), what happens to the app if you cancel, and whether they'll show you an app they got through Apple review recently. "Free" APK generators , including the ones behind "convert website to app mod apk" searches. These produce a basic WebView APK, often with their ads or branding inside, signed with a key you may never get. Losing the signing key means you can never update that Play listing. Never install a "mod" APK of one of these tools on your phone either: it's an unknown app asking for permissions. 5. Rebuild it as a native or cross-platform app If people will open the app every day, need it to be fast and smooth, or need deep device features (background location, Bluetooth, heavy offline data), build a real app. React Native and Flutter give you iPhone and Android from one codebase, while Swift and Kotlin give you one each. It doesn't reuse your website's pages, but it can reuse your website's back end: the same database, the same logins, through an API. This is also why I build websites with a separate API where a client might want an app later. The app then becomes a second front end, not a second system. A site with its logic locked inside the page templates (as many WordPress and page-builder sites are) needs that API written first. WordPress, Shopify, Wix and Squarespace sites People search for these by name, so briefly: WordPress: any of the methods above work. A PWA plugin is the quick path. For a store app, the converter services with WordPress plugins (method 4) or a Capacitor app on the WordPress REST API are the usual routes. Shopify: Shopify's App Store has mobile-app builder apps that turn a store into a store-listed app. That's method 4, built for Shopify. Wix and Squarespace: site builders give you little control over the files at your domain's root, and a TWA needs one there ( /.well-known/assetlinks.json ). Check that before you start. Wix also has its own branded-app product. Otherwise, a converter service is the realistic choice. Which one is best? For most business websites, my order is: Always do the PWA first. It costs a manifest and some icons, it improves the website for everyone, and both later options need it anyway (a TWA requires it, and a wrapper benefits from it). Need to be in Google Play? Add a TWA. It's the cheapest store app there is, and it updates itself every time the website changes. Need the App Store? Use Capacitor with real native features, or a converter service if there's no developer. Budget for review rejections the first time. Is the app the product? Rebuild natively or with React Native or Flutter, on your site's API. One thing before any of this: an app is only as good as the website inside it. A slow, clunky mobile site makes a slow, clunky app, and in a PWA, TWA or wrapper the speed is exactly the website's speed. Fix that first. Our website speed test and the Core Web Vitals guide are a good place to start, and this is what got this site to 100 on mobile . Quick checklist Manifest linked on every page, with name, start_url , display: standalone and 192 + 512 px icons. Apple touch icon for iPhone home screens. Service worker if you want offline pages or push. For Google Play: a TWA, /.well-known/assetlinks.json with the Play signing fingerprint, and two weeks for closed testing on a new personal account. For the App Store: native features, not just your URL in a frame. You own the developer accounts and the signing keys, whoever builds the app. FAQ Can I turn my website into an app for free? Yes, as an installable web app (PWA): add a web app manifest and icons, and people can install it from Chrome, Edge or Safari's Add to Home Screen at no cost. Getting into Google Play costs Google's one-time $25 developer fee, and the App Store needs Apple's $99 a year developer programme. What is the best way to convert a website into an app? For most business websites: make it a PWA first, then add a Trusted Web Activity if you need Google Play, and a Capacitor app with real native features if you need the App Store. Rebuild natively only when the app itself is the product and people will use it daily. Will Apple accept a WebView app? Only if it does more than the website. Apple's guideline 4.2 (Minimum Functionality) rejects apps that are a repackaged website. Wrapped apps that pass usually add native navigation, push notifications, device features such as camera or Face ID, and a proper offline screen. Does Google Play allow WebView apps? Google Play's spam policy rejects apps that are only a website in a WebView, and apps that wrap someone else's website without permission. For your own site, a Trusted Web Activity is Google's supported route: it shows your PWA full screen through Chrome and is verified with Digital Asset Links. Do I need a service worker to make my website installable? Not for the install prompt in current Chrome. I checked this site in Chrome 157: it was installable with only a manifest and icons and no service worker. You still need a service worker for offline pages and push notifications. Why does my TWA app show an address bar? The Digital Asset Links check failed, so Chrome fell back to a Custom Tab. Check that /.well-known/assetlinks.json is reachable and that it holds the SHA-256 fingerprint of the key that actually signs the app. With Play App Signing, that is the key shown in Play Console. Can a website app send push notifications on iPhone? Yes, since iOS 16.4, but only after the user adds the web app to the Home Screen and then allows notifications from a button tap inside it. A website open in a normal Safari tab cannot ask for push permission on iPhone. Originally published on knowledgemarkg.com .

title: MCP Failure Alerts: Know When Your MCP Server Breaks
author: Docstar
summary: When an AI assistant calls your MCP server and something on your side breaks, nobody tells you. The assistant gets an error, maybe retries, and then tells your user "that didn't work". Your user gives up, and you find out days later, if at all. DocStar's MCP failure alerts fix that: the moment a tool, your token check or your sign-in fails for one of your users, you get an alert on your own webhooks, in a Slack channel or by email, with the request that failed and the response your API gave. This post explains why MCP failures are so easy to miss, what a useful alert should contain, and how to turn alerts on for your DocStar MCP server in a couple of minutes. Why MCP failures go unnoticed A normal API has a dashboard, error logs and users who email support. An MCP server sits between an AI assistant and your API, and that changes who sees the error: The user never sees your error message. The AI assistant reads it and rephrases it, often as a vague apology. The assistant hides the pattern. It may retry, try a different tool, or give up quietly. One broken endpoint can look like the AI "being bad at your product". Sign-in failures look like the user's fault. If your token check refuses every token after a deploy, every user is asked to sign in again, and most simply stop using the connector. So the people who could fix the problem, you and your team, are the last to know. What a useful MCP alert contains An alert that just says "tool failed" sends you digging through logs. A useful one answers five questions straight away: Question Example What happened? "create_order" failed: your API answered 422 What did my users see? The AI got the error back and told the user the action failed. What should I do? A 4xx often means the AI called the tool with wrong inputs: check the tool's description and input examples. Which call failed, exactly? The request sent ( POST https://api.acme.com/v1/orders with its body) and the response (422 in 312 ms, with its body). How often? First time in the last 10 minutes, or "7 more since the last alert". It also has to be safe to send to a chat channel. Passwords, tokens, API keys, cookies and login codes must never end up in Slack. How failure alerts work in DocStar Every DocStar docs and API collection gets its own hosted MCP server. With failure alerts on, that server watches three things on your side: Tools. Your API answers 4xx or 5xx, can't be reached, or a tool's viaSocket flow fails. Your token check. If your MCP server checks users' tokens against your own validation URL, you're told when that URL fails, times out or refuses tokens. Sign-in. Your token URL refuses a login code or refresh, your session exchange fails, or your login page sends users back with an error. Each alert includes what happened, what your users saw, what to do, the API that failed, the request sent and the response received. Secret-looking values show as [hidden] , query strings are removed from URLs, and request headers are never included. To keep the noise down, the same problem is sent at most once every 10 minutes, and the next alert says how many times it happened in between. Problems on DocStar's side, and users who simply haven't signed in yet, never trigger an alert. Where alerts go Pick any mix of three places: Your webhooks. Add up to 9 https URLs. Each gets a POST with the alert as JSON, ready for your incident tool, your own Slack bot or a workflow. The JSON includes a ready-to-read message plus separate fields such as kind , api , request and response . Slack. Connect your workspace and pick a channel. Alerts arrive as a message in that channel. Email. Add up to 20 addresses, with nothing to connect. Alerts arrive from DocStar ( docstar-report@viasocket.com ), and each address gets its own copy, so no one sees the others. Turn it on Open your collection's settings and open the MCP tab. Under Server settings , click Set up next to Failure alerts . Add a webhook, connect Slack or add email addresses. Click Send test alert to check every destination. You see the result for each one. That's it. The next time something on your side breaks for an AI assistant user, you hear about it first. Full details, including the complete webhook payload, are in the Help page: MCP Failure Alerts: Webhooks, Slack and Email . Frequently asked questions Will I get flooded if my API goes down? No. Each problem is sent at most once every 10 minutes, with a count of repeats. Can I send alerts to more than one place? Yes. Add several webhooks, a Slack channel and several email addresses together. Every alert goes to all of them, and one failing destination doesn't stop the others. Are my users' tokens or passwords ever included? No. Values whose name looks like a password, token, API key, cookie or code are hidden, query strings are removed and request headers are never sent. Building an MCP server for your API? Start with DocStar and turn your API docs into an MCP server any AI assistant can use, with failure alerts built in. Originally published on the DocStar blog .
